Mode & Raga Library

Ragas, melakartas, maqamat, pathet, Japanese and church modes and jazz chord-scales, each split into what is fixed (like a clave), what is chosen from a pool (like bebop alterations), where it leans, and what is left free; every card plays, and every note comes from a cited source.

The Rhythm Library collects patterns that repeat exactly: play son clave backwards and it is no longer son clave. Melody systems are different. Some parts work like that clave, and others work like the alterations on a bebop dominant, where the player picks ♭9 or ♯9 tonight and something else tomorrow. Each card below sorts a mode’s features into four kinds:

What it means Like…
Fixed Change it and it is no longer this mode. the clave: one pattern, kept exactly
Chosen The tradition gives a set; the player picks from it each time. bebop alterations: any of ♭9 ♯9 ♯11 ♭13
Leans on Weight and habit: stressed notes, usual endings. A centre, not a rule. the backbeat on 2 and 4
Free Left to the musician: the tunes, the ornaments, the order of ideas. a solo

Strict and chosen, tradition by tradition

Tradition Fixed Chosen Leans on Free
Hindustani rāg the notes, the way up and the way down (āroh / avaroh), crooked (vakra) paths, special intonation (little: each rāg’s notes and turns are set) vādī and saṁvādī, stressed and passing notes the tunes (“an infinite number”), ornaments, the order of the performance
Karnatak mela all seven notes, stepwise, the same both ways: a rule that fixes all 72 compositions, improvisation
Karnatak janya rāga which notes are left out, where it turns back
Arabic maqām the lower jins and the ghammaz the upper jins (Rast: Upper Rast or Nahawand) intonation (quarter tones are notation, not pitch) modulation, the path (sayr)
Javanese pathet the gamelan’s own tuning stressed tones, avoided endings the elaborating parts
Japanese in / yo the five notes auxiliary notes, used or not the nuclear tones a fourth apart
Church modes the final and the range the reciting tone the chant
Jazz the bebop scale’s passing note, so chord tones land on the beat alterations on 7alt; which scale over a dominant the line

Choose a tonic, a sound and a tempo here; every ▶ on the page uses them. Rāgs and maqāmat play over a drone (Sa and Pa, or Sa and Ma when the rāg has no Pa, as Garland describes); jazz cards play their chord on the piano. A 🎲 picks from a pool for you.

Hindustani rāg

A rāg “is not a tune … it is not a scale, because numerous ragas can be based on the same scale” (Ruckert and Widdess 67). Its āroh and avaroh are often different, “since different pitches may appear in ascending and descending contexts”, and may leave strict scale order (vakra, crooked). Performers know a rāg mainly by its phrases: the calan (“way of moving”) and the pakaḍ (“catch”, the phrase that sums it up). Playing another rāg’s phrase by accident “is regarded as a gross error” (68-69).

The 23 below are Garland’s Figure 6 (80-81), exactly as printed, grouped as there: dawn and sunset rāgs (sandhiprakāś), the bilāval family (major-scale tones), the āsāvarī family (natural-minor tones), four with one outline in different forms of the notes, and three for the rainy season. Lower case = komal (flat), M = tīvra Ma (sharp 4th); a dot above or below = the upper or lower register; a gap = a breath in the printed line. The notes are tuned in pure ratios against the drone, as on the Ragas lesson; Garland says real intonation “cannot be reduced to a rigid system” (67).

Karnatak rāga

Venkatamakhi (17th century) set three rules for a parent (mela) rāga: all seven notes going up and coming down, in stepwise order, with the same intervals both ways (Kassebaum 97). With two forms of Ma and six ways each to fill Ri–Ga and Dha–Ni, the rule gives 72 melas, and each is completely fixed by it. Derived (janya) rāgas leave notes out, turn back, or add notes from outside. Musicians “do not study the system directly”: they learn rāgas from compositions (97).

Build any of the 72

The numbering here (Ma, then Ri–Ga pair, then Dha–Ni pair) is worked out from the rule; only mela 29’s name is checked.

Arabic maqām

A jins is “a maqam scale fragment of 3, 4 or 5 notes”. A maqām starts with one jins on its tonic, which names its family, and continues with another from the ghammaz, “the most important note of melodic emphasis (besides the tonic)” (MaqamWorld). For many maqāmat MaqamWorld names two possible upper ajnas: that is the chosen part. The quarter-tone numbers are notation: Wikipedia says the 24-tone system “does not affect the actual precise intonation of the notes performed”. The cents here are that notation, not a performer’s tuning.

Javanese pathet

Each tuning has three pathet: slendro nem, sanga and manyura, and pélog lima, nem and barang. These are the “tonic”, the “dominant” and the avoided notes from Wikipedia’s table. It adds that the avoided notes are “rare as seleh” (phrase endings). Nothing is fixed about the pitches across gamelans: “no two gamelan sets will have exactly the same tuning” (Lindsay, via Wikipedia). Within one gamelan, though, every instrument shares them, so the tuning is fixed for the players.

Japanese scales

Church modes

A mode in plainchant is set by its final and its range. Each authentic mode has a plagal partner on the same final, a fourth lower. Psalm verses are chanted on the reciting tone.

Jazz: bebop and chord-scales

These are the opposite cases. The bebop scale’s added passing note is placed so that “the primary chord tones … continuously fall on the on-beats” (Wikipedia, “Bebop scale”): that placement is fixed, like a clave. An altered dominant is a pool: the alterations of a “G7alt” are “left to the artistic discretion of the comping musician” (Wikipedia, “Altered chord”).

Not here yet

  • Turkish makam, Persian dastgāh: no source read yet. The Garland volume on the Middle East is the next place to look.
  • Maqām notes and paths as MaqamWorld draws them: its scales, ascents and descents, and sayr are images, not text, so only the structure in its prose is here. Saba’s measured cents (160, 140 and 95 for its first steps, Wikipedia) are not used yet.
  • Pakaḍ phrases for each rāg: Garland gives no pakaḍ for these rāgs. Vādī and saṁvādī are left out for the same reason (sources for both: scripts/sources/ragas.py).
  • Pūrvīkalyāṇī and other janya rāgas in Kassebaum’s Figure 6: the notes in the scan are not yet read.
  • Melakarta names other than 29: not checked.
  • Pathet and time of night: Wikipedia gives only the order through a wayang.
  • Gamaka: Karnatak ornaments are part of the notes themselves, and these plain players do not play them.

Works Cited

“Acoustic scale.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acoustic_scale. Lydian dominant over 7#11.

“Altered chord.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altered_chord. 7alt; alterations left to the comping musician.

“Altered scale.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altered_scale.

“Arabic maqam.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_maqam. Quarter tones as notation, not precise intonation; modulation.

“Bebop scale.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop_scale. Passing note placed so chord tones fall on the beats; David Baker’s name.

“Chord-scale system.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chord-scale_system.

Farraj, Johnny, and Sami Abu Shumays. Maqam World, www.maqamworld.com/en/. Accessed 27 Nov. 2026. Maqam pages Rast, Bayati, Hijaz, Saba, Nahawand, Kurd (lower jins, ghammaz, upper ajnas); jins pages (sizes, Hijaz’s second played smaller than notated).

“Hirajōshi scale.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hirajōshi_scale. Three versions in three sets of sources, one interval pattern.

“In scale.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_scale.

Kassebaum, Gayathri Rajapur. “Karnatak Raga.” The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 5, South Asia: The Indian Subcontinent, edited by Alison Arnold, Garland, 2000, pp. 89-109. Pp. 97-98: Venkatamakhi’s 72 melas and the three rules for a parent raga; janya ragas; Fig. 6 Madhyamavati.

“Mode (music).” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mode_(music). Church modes: finals, reciting tones, authentic and plagal ranges.

“Octatonic scale.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octatonic_scale. Half-whole diminished in dominant harmony.

“Pathet.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pathet. Table of tonic, dominant and avoided tones; Hood’s cadences ‘largely disproven’.

“Pelog.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelog. 9-TET subset as a rough approximation (Surjodiningrat); tones of each pathet.

Ruckert, George, and Richard Widdess. “Hindustani Raga.” The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 5, South Asia: The Indian Subcontinent, edited by Alison Arnold, Garland, 2000, pp. 64-88. Pp. 67-69 (a raga neither tune nor scale; aroh / avaroh, vakra; vadi / samvadi and their limits; calan, pakad; a wrong raga’s phrase a gross error; drone Ma or Ni when no Pa), p. 75 and Fig. 4 (Darbari’s straight descent a violation; Jaunpuri), Fig. 6 pp. 80-81 (23 ragas’ aroh and avaroh), pp. 81-82 (andolan).

“Slendro.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slendro. Roughly equal steps; no two gamelans alike (Lindsay).

“Yo scale.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yo_scale.
